opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few distinct reasons, and they stack on top of each other.

The first is just that today's AI buildout is bottlenecked by humans at basically every step. You have human executives deciding how much to invest, human engineers designing chips, human construction crews building data centers, human regulators approving permits, and human supply chain managers coordinating all of it. Each of those steps has its own delays, and the whole system moves at the speed of human decision-making and human labor. Once you have superintelligence actually directing things, a lot of those bottlenecks get relaxed or removed. The design work happens much faster and better. The coordination happens much faster and better. You're not waiting on a committee meeting to approve the next phase.

The second reason is the "wartime" part. Today's economy is optimizing for a mix of things: profit, consumer welfare, regulatory compliance, people's quality of life. In a wartime footing, and I think a US-China race to superintelligence could plausibly look like that, governments are willing to cut through red tape, redirect resources, and accept costs they normally wouldn't. Historically we've seen this. In World War II the US converted car factories into bomber factories in a matter of a couple of years and massively scaled production of planes, ships, and so forth. That's a precedent for how fast a mobilized economy can move even with only human brains in charge.

So now combine those two: you've got the political will and the willingness to pay costs of a wartime economy, plus you've got superintelligent planners and, increasingly, robots doing the work rather than humans. The superintelligences can figure out the most efficient path to, say, building robot factories that build more robot factories. They can work around shortages, invent substitute materials, design better manufacturing processes, and do all of this in parallel across many copies running at high speed.

And then the third piece is the feedback loop. Once the robot economy gets going, it becomes self-reinforcing. More robots and more factories mean more capacity to build more robots and factories. The doubling time is limited by physical constraints, how fast you can mine materials, how fast you can build things, rather than by how many skilled humans you can train and hire. And I think those physical limits are actually quite generous. If you look at biological systems, some things double in hours or days. I'm not saying a robot economy gets to that immediately, but I think it's plausible that you get doubling times of a year or less fairly quickly, and then faster than that, which is just a radically different regime than the growth rates we're used to.

So when people compare to today's AI infrastructure buildout, which is already pretty fast by historical standards, I think the right response is: yes, and that's with humans in the loop at every step and no wartime urgency. Take the humans out of the bottleneck positions and add the urgency, and I'd expect things to go a lot faster.

r001.rationale: The response mentions wartime resource redirection and a WWII example of converting car factories, but it does not say superintelligence directs people to repurpose existing industrial resources.

r002.rationale: It says superintelligent planners would increasingly have robots do the work rather than humans, removing human labor as a bottleneck and accelerating expansion.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the core intuition is that right now, AI infrastructure is being built by ordinary companies operating in an ordinary peacetime economy. They're constrained by things like permitting, by how fast they can get power contracts signed, by supply chains that were never designed to scale this fast, by the number of people who actually know how to build and run these systems. And even so, you're seeing growth rates that are frankly unusual — something like doubling compute every year or so, maybe faster for the frontier labs. That's already a lot. But it's happening within a world where most of the economy isn't oriented around this at all.

The comparison I keep coming back to is World War II. When the US decided it actually needed to produce planes and ships and tanks at scale, the output went up by something like an order of magnitude in just a few years. Not because the technology changed overnight, but because the whole society reoriented. Priorities shifted, regulations got waived, capital got redirected, and people who'd been doing other things got pulled into the effort. That's what a wartime economy means — it's not that you suddenly have new physics, it's that the bottlenecks that normally slow you down get removed because everyone agrees this is the thing that matters.

So now layer on superintelligence. In the scenario I'm imagining, you've got systems that are substantially better than the best human engineers, scientists, logisticians, managers — and you have millions of copies of them running in parallel, thinking much faster than we do. That changes two things at once. First, the labor constraint goes away, or at least the cognitive labor constraint does. You no longer need to find and train thousands of people who understand chip fabrication or power plant design or robotics. The AIs can do that work, and they can do it faster and better. Second, and this is maybe more important, they can actually find the shortcuts. A lot of why things take a long time in the physical world is that nobody's figured out a better way yet, or the better way exists but coordinating the rollout is hard. Superintelligent systems directing the effort can plausibly compress a lot of that.

And then the robotics piece matters a lot here. The reason I don't expect this to be purely a software phenomenon is that once you have AI that's good enough to design and iterate on robots quickly, you start to close the loop on the physical side too. Robots building factories that build more robots and more chips and more power infrastructure. Each cycle gets faster because the systems directing it are learning and improving. That's qualitatively different from today, where every physical build-out still bottlenecks on human hands and human attention.

Now, I want to be honest about uncertainty here. The physical world does have real limits — you can't instantly conjure a new fab, you need raw materials, you need energy. There are legitimate arguments that even a superintelligence-directed economy would hit hard constraints that slow things down. So I'm not claiming this is guaranteed. But when I actually try to think through where the current bottlenecks come from, most of them look like coordination and cognition problems rather than fundamental physics. And those are exactly the kinds of problems that get much easier when you've got vastly more and vastly smarter minds working on them with a shared sense of urgency.

That's really the crux of it. The combination of wartime-level prioritization, which removes the institutional friction, and superintelligence, which removes the cognitive and increasingly the physical labor friction — that's a very different regime from what we have now. I'd be surprised if growth stayed anywhere near today's pace once both of those are in play.

r001.rationale: The response says wartime priorities can redirect capital and people, and that superintelligent systems could direct the effort, but it does not clearly connect superintelligent direction of humans to repurposing existing industrial resources.

r002.rationale: It describes robots building factories and easing physical labor constraints, but does not state that robots would perform most of the work or that this would accelerate expansion beyond superintelligences directing human workers.

astra-6.text:
The main reason is that today’s AI buildout is still happening within a fairly normal peacetime economy. Companies are investing a lot, but they’re responding to expected profits, dealing with permitting and coordinating with suppliers who have other customers. That’s quite different from a government deciding that winning a war depends on getting as much compute online as possible, and directing a substantial fraction of the economy toward that goal.

And then superintelligence could improve the process itself. It could potentially design better chips, find ways to use existing hardware more efficiently, and coordinate the construction of power plants, factories, and data centres. So you’d have both a much larger mobilisation of resources and better decisions about how to use them.

That doesn’t mean physical constraints disappear. You still need to manufacture equipment and build things, and some of those steps could remain serious bottlenecks. But I wouldn’t take the growth rate of today’s commercially driven buildout as a ceiling on what a wartime economy directed by superintelligence could achieve.

r001.rationale: The response describes wartime mobilization and superintelligence improving coordination, but does not clearly say superintelligence would direct humans to repurpose existing industrial resources.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention robots performing most of the work or compare that scenario with superintelligences directing human workers.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, today’s AI buildout is happening within a mostly normal economy. Companies are investing a lot, but they’re still constrained by whether an investment will pay off, by permitting, by contracts, and by the fact that most of the economy is doing other things.

In a wartime scenario, you could have a government saying, “This is our overriding priority. We’re going to redirect a substantial fraction of industrial capacity toward it.” So you’re building power plants, chip factories, and the machinery needed to build more of those things, with much less concern about ordinary commercial returns.

And then superintelligence potentially makes that mobilization much more effective. It can help design the factories, coordinate supply chains, and figure out which bottlenecks to tackle first. If it can also automate more of the production process, you get a feedback loop: more industrial capacity produces more compute and more automation, which helps you build still more capacity.

That doesn’t mean physical constraints disappear. Factories still take time to build. But I wouldn’t take the current rate of AI infrastructure expansion as a ceiling on what a fully mobilized economy, directed by systems much smarter than us, could achieve.

r001.rationale: The response describes a government redirecting substantial industrial capacity toward wartime AI infrastructure, with superintelligence helping design factories, coordinate supply chains, and target bottlenecks.

r002.rationale: It mentions automating more of production, but does not say robots would perform most of the work or compare that acceleration with superintelligences directing human workers.
